mainTopic: Who bears the loss when hired work is cut short, and how workers who quit midway are paid
overview: This amud deals with hired workers whose work is cut short. רבא gives a series of rulings. If the employer should have foreseen the problem, such as a rising river or a field he did not check, he bears the loss and pays the workers as a פועל בטל. If no one could have expected it, or the local workers knew the risk, the workers bear the loss. When a job ends early, the employer may assign only easier or equal work. The גמרא then explains a ברייתא about workers who quit in the middle of a job. The רבנן say the worker has the upper hand, and each 'obvious' line is shown to teach something about pay claims when prices change. רבי דוסא says the worker who backs out takes the loss, and רב rules like him. The גמרא then asks how this fits with רב's own view that a worker may quit even midday, and begins a ברייתא that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Finishing the rule about rain and checking the field
steps.stepSummary: The end of רבא's ruling from the previous page: if the employer checked his field the night before, the loss is the workers'. If he did not check, the loss is his, and he pays them as a פועל בטל.
steps.simpleTranslation: …it is the workers' loss. If he did not check his land the night before, it is the employer's loss, and he pays them the wage of an idle worker.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a ruling of רבא that began on the previous page. Whether the employer checked his field the night before decides who loses when rain stops the work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the employer checked the field and it was fine, the rain was a surprise to everyone, so the workers bear the loss. If he never checked, the problem might have been visible already, so the fault is his. He then pays them as a פועל בטל, a reduced wage, because they did not actually work.

keyTerms.meaning: an idle worker; the lower wage a worker would accept to sit and not work

steps.confusionAlert: Paying 'like a פועל בטל' does not mean full pay. It is a reduced amount, since the worker was spared the effort of working.

phrases.english: it is the workers' loss.
phrases.notes: This ends רבא's ruling from the previous page: the employer checked his field the night before, and then rain stopped the work.

phrases.english: If he did not check his land the night before,
it is the employer's loss,
and he gives them pay like an idle worker.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רבא's ruling that began on the previous page.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Checked field: workers' loss. Unchecked field: employer's loss, and he pays them as a פועל בטל.

steps.title: Workers hired to irrigate: rain versus a rising river
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules about workers hired to draw water. If rain waters the field, the workers lose. If the river rises and waters it, the employer loses and pays them as a פועל בטל.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Someone who hired workers to draw water, and rain came, it is the workers' loss. If the river came up, it is the employer's loss, and he pays them as idle workers.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a new ruling. Workers were hired to water a field, and the job became unnecessary in one of two ways.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Rain is a surprise that neither side could have planned for, so the workers bear the loss. A rising river is something the employer should have taken into account before hiring, so the fault is his. He pays them the reduced wage of a פועל בטל.

keyTerms.meaning: drawing water to irrigate, by bucket or water wheel

phrases.english: And Rava said:
Someone who hires workers to draw water for irrigation,
and rain came,
it is the workers' loss.
If the river came up,
phrases.notes: He means the river rose and watered the field by itself, so no one needed to draw water.

phrases.english: it is the employer's loss,
and he gives them pay like an idle worker.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רָבָא: הַאי מַאן דְּאוֹגַיר אֲגִירֵי לְדַוְולָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another ruling of רבא that uses the same idea of who could have foreseen the problem.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Rain: workers' loss. Rising river: employer's loss, and he pays them as a פועל בטל.

steps.title: The river stopped flowing in the middle of the day
steps.stepSummary: If the river stops midday, it depends. If it does not usually stop, the workers lose. If it usually stops, local workers lose because they knew, and outside workers do not, so the employer loses.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Someone who hired workers to draw water, and the river stopped in the middle of the day: if it does not usually stop, it is the workers' loss. If it usually stops: if they are from the town, it is the workers' loss. If they are not from the town, it is the employer's loss.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a third ruling. This time the water source dried up halfway through the day, so the work could not go on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the river does not usually stop, the stoppage was a surprise to everyone, so the workers lose. If it usually stops, the question is who knew it. Local workers knew and accepted the risk, so they lose. Outsiders could not know, and the employer should have warned them, so he loses.

keyTerms.meaning: it usually stops; it tends to stop

steps.whyThisMatters: This ruling shows that the workers' knowledge counts too. A risk that the workers knew about when they took the job can be their loss.

phrases.english: And Rava said:
Someone who hires workers to draw water for irrigation,
and the river stopped flowing in the middle of the day:
if it does not usually stop,
it is the workers' loss.
If it usually stops,
if they are people of the town, it is the workers' loss.

phrases.aramaic: לָאו בְּנֵי מָתָא – פְּסֵידָא דְּבַעַל הַבַּיִת.
phrases.english: If they are not people of the town, it is the employer's loss.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רָבָא: הַאי מַאן דְּאוֹגַיר אֲגִירֵי לְדַוְולָא, וּפְסַק נַהֲרָא בְּפַלְגָא דְיוֹמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same irrigation setting as step 2, but now the river stops instead of rising, and the workers' knowledge becomes a factor.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: River not prone to stopping: workers' loss. River prone to stopping: locals lose; with outsiders, the employer loses.

steps.title: The job was finished by midday
steps.stepSummary: If the job is done by midday, the employer may give the workers easier work or equal work for the rest of the day. He may not assign harder work, and he pays them their full wages.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Someone who hired workers for a job, and the job was finished in the middle of the day: if he has work easier than it, he gives it to them. Also work equal to it, he may assign them. Work harder than it, he may not assign them, and he pays them their full wages.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a fourth ruling. The work did not stop because of an outside event; the job was simply finished early.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The workers were hired for a full day, so the employer may use the rest of their day. He can only assign work that is easier than or equal to what they agreed to, because they never agreed to anything harder. If all he has is harder work, he cannot force it on them, and he pays them their full wages.
steps.whatToRemember: Across all of רבא's rulings, the question is who could have foreseen the problem. If the employer should have known, he bears the loss. If no one could have known, or the workers knew, the workers bear it. When the job ends early, the employer may assign only easier or equal work.

phrases.english: And Rava said:
Someone who hired workers for a job,
and the job was finished in the middle of the day:

phrases.aramaic: אִי אִית לֵיהּ עֲבִידְתָּא דְּנִיחָא מִינַּהּ –
phrases.english: if he has work that is easier than it,
he gives it to them;
also, work like it, he may assign to them;
work harder than it, he may not assign to them,
phrases.notes: The word in round brackets is the standard printed wording, and the word in square brackets is the corrected wording. Both mean 'harder.'

phrases.english: and he gives them their full wages.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רָבָא: הַאי מַאן דַּאֲגַר אֲגִירֵי לַעֲבִידְתָּא, וּשְׁלִים עֲבִידְתָּא בְּפַלְגָא דְיוֹמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from outside events that stop the work to a job that simply ends early.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the job ends early, the employer may assign easier or equal work. He may not assign harder work, and he pays full wages.

steps.title: Why full wages and not the idle worker's rate?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבא's ruling from Step 4 that workers who finish early get their full wage.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why does he pay them full wages? Let him pay them like a פועל בטל, an idle worker!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבא's ruling that the employer pays full wages for the rest of the day. It asks why he does not pay them the lower rate of a פועל בטל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, when workers could not work at all, רבא said they get paid as a פועל בטל, a lower rate, since they get to rest. So here too, for the hours after the job is done, the employer should only owe that lower rate.

keyTerms.meaning: An idle worker, who is paid less because he gets to rest

phrases.english: Why?
phrases.notes: Why does the employer pay full wages for the rest of the day, as רבא said in Step 4?

phrases.english: Let him pay them as an idle worker!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's full-wage ruling from Step 4
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's ruling that workers who finish by midday get full pay
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Elsewhere רבא only gives the lower פועל בטל rate for time not worked, so the same should apply here.

steps.title: רבא meant the workers of מחוזא
steps.stepSummary: The workers רבא spoke about get weak when they sit idle, so resting is no benefit for them.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רבא said this, he was talking about the workers of מחוזא, who become weak if they do not work.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבא's ruling was about the workers of מחוזא. For them, sitting idle is not a pleasant break.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פועל בטל rate is lower because resting is worth something to the worker. These workers are used to hard, steady work, so sitting around makes them weak. Since idleness gives them no benefit, nothing is taken off their pay.

keyTerms.meaning: מחוזא, a busy town where רבא lived

phrases.english: When Rava said it,
it was about the workers of Mechoza,
who, if they do not work, become weak.

steps.whatToRemember: The lower פועל בטל rate only makes sense when resting actually helps the worker. For workers who get weak from sitting around, the employer pays full wages.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 5
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the ruling to a specific group of workers
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every worker who finishes early should get only the lower idle rate
steps.terutzMaskana: רבא's full-wage ruling is about workers for whom being idle is a hardship, not a benefit

steps.title: Workers who quit get paid for what they did
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the ברייתא about workers who quit in the middle: their work is valued, and they still get the original rate for it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: We value for them what they have done. How so? If the part they did is now worth six דינרים, he gives them a סלע. The רבנן hold that the worker has the upper hand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now turns to a ברייתא about workers who quit partway through a job and starts explaining it line by line. Even though the work they finished is now worth more, the employer gives them a סלע, which was the original rate.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The workers agreed to the whole job for two סלעים and did half. Prices went up, so their half is now worth six דינרים, a סלע and a half. They still get a סלע for it. Even though they backed out, they do not lose their pay, because the רבנן hold that the worker has the upper hand.

keyTerms.meaning: We value, we work out how much it is worth
The worker has the upper hand

phrases.english: The Master said:
phrases.notes: The גמרא is quoting a ברייתא about workers who agreed to a job for two סלעים, did half, and then quit.

phrases.aramaic: שָׁמִין לָהֶם אֶת מַה שֶּׁעָשׂוּ, כֵּיצַד?
phrases.english: We value for them what they have done. How so?
If it was worth six dinars,
phrases.notes: Prices went up, so the half they did now costs a סלע and a half to hire for.

phrases.english: he gives them a sela.
The Rabbis hold:
the hand of the worker is on top.

steps.confusionAlert: The 'six דינרים' is not what the workers are paid. It is what their half of the job is now worth on the market. They are paid one סלע, the original rate.
steps.whyThisMatters: The idea that the worker has the upper hand is a key rule for workers who quit: they do not lose the pay they already earned.
steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר מָר: שָׁמִין לָהֶם אֶת מַה שֶּׁעָשׂוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to explain a new ברייתא
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Workers who quit get the original rate for the work they did, because the worker has the upper hand.

steps.title: Finishing for two סלעים seems obvious
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא says the workers can finish and take two סלעים. The גמרא asks why that needs to be said.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or they finish their work and take two סלעים. That is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next line of the ברייתא: the workers may finish the job and take two סלעים. It asks why this needs saying, since that was the deal from the start.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The workers originally agreed to do the whole job for two סלעים. If they finish, of course they get two סלעים. So what new thing is this line teaching?

phrases.english: Or they finish their work
and take two selaim.
That is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues explaining the ברייתא and questions its next line
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's line 'or they finish and take two סלעים'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: That was the original agreement, so the line seems to teach nothing new.

steps.title: Coaxed workers cannot demand a raise
steps.stepSummary: The line is needed when workers stopped working and the employer won them back. He can say he meant better food and drink, not more money.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed where the cost of labor went up, the workers rebelled, and the employer went and calmed them down. You might think they can tell him: 'When we let you calm us down, it was on the understanding that you would raise our pay.' So the ברייתא teaches that he can tell them: 'I meant that I would go out of my way for you with food and drink.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the line is about workers who refused to keep working when prices went up, until the employer talked them back. The ברייתא teaches that they still get only two סלעים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The workers might claim the employer's coaxing meant he promised them more money. The employer can answer that he only meant to treat them well with food and drink. Since nothing clear was promised, the original pay of two סלעים stands.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for a special case
The cost of labor went up
They rebelled, they refused to keep working
He calmed them down, won them over

phrases.english: No, it is needed:
where labor became expensive and the workers rebelled
and the employer went and calmed them down.
You might say they can tell him:
When we let ourselves be calmed down,
it was on the understanding that you would add to our wage,
so it teaches us that he can tell them:
It was on the understanding that I would go out of my way for you
with food and drink.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא: דְּאִיַּיקַּר עֲבִידְתָּא וְאִימְּרוּ פּוֹעֲלִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'obvious' challenge of Step 8
steps.terutzResolutionType: Places the line in a specific, less obvious case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Workers who were coaxed back after rising prices could claim they were promised a raise
steps.terutzMaskana: The employer can say he meant better food and drink, so they get only the original two סלעים

steps.title: A סלע for a סלע's work seems obvious
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא says that if the work done is worth a סלע, he gives them a סלע. The גמרא asks why that needs saying.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it is worth a סלע, he gives them a סלע. That is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the last line of the ברייתא: if the half they did is worth a סלע, they get a סלע. It asks why this needs to be said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If prices did not change, half the job is worth exactly half the pay, one סלע. That seems too simple to need stating.

phrases.english: If it is worth a sela, he gives them a sela.
phrases.notes: The ברייתא means the half they finished is worth exactly one סלע on the market now.

phrases.english: That is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the next line of the same ברייתא
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's line 'if it is worth a סלע, he gives them a סלע'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Half the work for half the pay seems too simple to need saying.

steps.title: The case where they were hired above the going rate
steps.stepSummary: The line is needed where the workers were hired for a דינר more than the going rate, and later prices rose to match it.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed where labor was cheap at the start, and he hired them for one extra דינר, and in the end the cost of labor went up and reached that extra דינר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the line is about workers who were first hired for more than the going rate. Later, market prices rose to that same level.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At the start the workers got a דינר more than normal. When they quit, prices had risen so that their higher rate is now the normal rate, and the half they did is worth exactly a סלע. The next step explains the point: the workers cannot demand an extra דינר on top of that, and they get just the סלע.

keyTerms.meaning: One extra coin, one דינר more

phrases.english: No, it is needed
where labor was cheap at the start,
and he hired them for an extra dinar,
and in the end labor became expensive
and stood at the extra dinar.

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא about workers who quit: they get the original rate for the work they did, because the worker has the upper hand. If they finish, they get only the agreed pay, even if the employer coaxed them back. If they were hired above the going rate and prices later rose to match it, they get a סלע and cannot demand an extra דינר.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'obvious' challenge of Step 10
steps.terutzResolutionType: Places the line in a specific, less obvious case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The workers could demand one דינר above the new going rate, since they were originally promised one more than the going rate
steps.terutzMaskana: The extra דינר was only offered to win their agreement. Once the going rate rises to match it, the workers get one סלע for their half and nothing extra.

steps.title: The employer is not stuck adding the extra dinar again
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes the answer from step 11. It explains what the workers might have claimed, and why the employer can turn them down.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might think the workers can say: 'You promised us a זוז more than the going rate, so give us a זוז more now too.' The ברייתא teaches that he can answer: 'I offered an extra זוז only because back then I wasn't sure you would agree to work. Now you have agreed, so there is no need.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes explaining why the line about giving a סלע is needed. It spells out the mistaken idea the ברייתא is coming to reject.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At the start, the workers were hired for one דינר above the going rate. Later the going rate rose to match what they were being paid. The workers might claim they always deserve one more than the going rate. The employer answers that the extra was only to get them to agree, so they get what was agreed and nothing more.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have thought (the mistaken idea that the teaching comes to reject)
It teaches us (the actual new point)
One extra זוז (a coin worth one דינר)
You are settled / you have agreed to it

phrases.english: You might have said that they can say to him:
"You promised us one zuz extra,
phrases.notes: A זוז is the same coin as a דינר. 'Extra' means above the going rate, as in step 11.

phrases.english: so give us one zuz extra now too."
It teaches us that he can say to them:
"When I told you one zuz extra,
it was because you had not yet agreed;
now you have agreed."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the תירוץ of step 11 by stating the mistaken idea and the חידוש.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the hidden mistaken idea (מהו דתימא) that the line rejects
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The workers might claim they always deserve one דינר above whatever the going rate is.
steps.terutzMaskana: The extra דינר was only to win their agreement. Once the going rate matches it, they get exactly what was agreed.

steps.title: רבי דוסא: value what is left to do; the worker takes the loss
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא brings רבי דוסא's opinion: the court values the work still left to do. The גמרא explains that he holds the worker who backs out takes the loss.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי דוסא says: We value the work that still has to be done. If it is worth six דינרים, the employer gives the workers a שקל. The גמרא explains that he holds the worker is at a disadvantage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues quoting the ברייתא, now with רבי דוסא's opinion about workers who quit in the middle. It then adds one line explaining his reasoning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of valuing what the workers already did, רבי דוסא looks at what it will cost to hire others to finish. That cost is taken out of the original two סלעים, and the quitting workers get whatever is left. This comes from the rule that the worker who backs out is on the losing side.

keyTerms.meaning: They value / assess (the court sets a price)
A coin worth half a סלע (two דינרים)
The worker is at a disadvantage (he takes the loss)
He holds (the reason behind his opinion)

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up a second opinion in the ברייתא. The next lines of the ברייתא, which the גמרא now examines, all follow רבי דוסא's approach.

phrases.english: Rabbi Dosa says:
They value for them that which
still has to be done.
If it was worth six dinars,
he gives them a shekel.
phrases.notes: A סלע is four דינרים, so six דינרים is a סלע and a half. Two סלעים minus that leaves half a סלע, which is a שקל.

phrases.english: He holds that the worker's hand is on the bottom.
phrases.notes: Literally 'on the lower side.' It means the worker is the one who takes the loss.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the first opinion in the ברייתא to רבי דוסא's opinion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Value the work still left to do and take that cost out of the agreed wage. The worker who backs out takes the loss.

steps.title: Why say they can finish and take two סלעים?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא lets the workers finish their job and take the full two סלעים. The גמרא asks why that needs to be said.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Or they finish their work and take two סלעים.' Isn't that obvious?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes another line of רבי דוסא's opinion and challenges it as obvious.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the workers do the whole job, of course they get the full wage they agreed on. So why does the ברייתא bother to say so?

keyTerms.meaning: It's obvious! (why does this need to be said?)
סלעים, silver coins worth four דינרים each

phrases.english: Or they finish their work
and take two sela'im.
That's obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Examines the next line of רבי דוסא's opinion.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's line 'or they finish their work and take two סלעים'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Workers who finish the job obviously get the agreed wage, so the line seems unnecessary.

steps.title: Workers who calmed down an angry employer still get full pay
steps.stepSummary: The line is needed where the price of labor dropped, the employer wanted to back out, and the workers calmed him down. He cannot claim they agreed to take less pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: It's needed where labor got cheaper, the employer rebelled, and the workers went and calmed him down. You might think he can say: 'I agreed because I thought you would take less pay.' The ברייתא teaches that they can answer: 'We meant that we would do excellent work for you.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by describing a special case where the line teaches something new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once labor got cheaper, the employer wanted to get out of the higher wage. When the workers won him back, he might claim they had quietly agreed to a pay cut. The ברייתא teaches that they can say they only promised better work, so the full two סלעים stand.

keyTerms.meaning: He rebelled / tried to back out
They calmed him down / won him over

steps.confusionAlert: This is the same kind of argument as step 9, but turned around. There the employer said he meant better food and drink. Here the workers say they meant better work, not less pay.

phrases.english: No, it is needed where labor became cheaper
and the employer rebelled,
and the workers went and calmed him down.
You might have said he can say to them:
"It was with the understanding that you would cut down my payment."
It teaches us that they can say to him:
"It was with the understanding that we would do for you
excellent work."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the פשיטא of step 14 by setting up a specific case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the line to a special case (לא צריכא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The employer could say that calming him down meant the workers agreed to a pay cut.
steps.terutzMaskana: The workers can say they only promised better work, so they get the full two סלעים.

steps.title: Why say 'if it is worth a סלע, he gives a סלע'?
steps.stepSummary: רבי דוסא says that if the work left to do is worth a סלע, the employer gives the workers a סלע. The גמרא asks why that needs saying.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'If a סלע, he gives them a סלע.' Isn't that obvious?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next line of רבי דוסא and challenges it as obvious.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If finishing the job costs one סלע, taking that out of the two סלעים plainly leaves one סלע for the workers. This follows directly from his rule, so the line seems unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: A silver coin worth four דינרים

phrases.english: If a sela, he gives them a sela.
phrases.notes: Meaning: if the work still left to do is worth a סלע, the workers get a סלע for what they did.

phrases.english: That's obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next line of רבי דוסא's opinion with another פשיטא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי דוסא's line 'if a סלע, he gives them a סלע'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The result follows simply from his rule, so why state it?

steps.title: רב הונא בריה דרב נתן: the workers took a discount at first, then prices dropped
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא בריה דרב נתן says the line is needed where the workers agreed at the start to a דינר below the going rate, and later the price of labor dropped.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא the son of רב נתן said: It's needed where the workers lowered their price for him by a זוז at the start, and in the end the price of labor dropped.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts answering the challenge by describing the case where the line is needed. This line sets up the case; the explanation of what it teaches comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This case is the mirror image of step 11. There the workers were hired for a דינר above the going rate. Here they agreed to a דינר below it, and later the going rate dropped to match their wage.

keyTerms.meaning: They lowered the price (gave a discount)

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב נָתָן:
phrases.english: Rav Huna the son of Rav Natan said:
No, it is needed where they lowered
the price for him by a zuz at the start,
and in the end labor became cheaper.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב נָתָן: לָא צְרִיכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the פשיטא of step 16 by setting up a specific case. The explanation of what it teaches continues afterward.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the line to a special case (לא צריכא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Not yet stated; the גמרא spells it out in the next line.
steps.terutzMaskana: The line applies where the workers took a one-דינר discount at the start and the going rate later dropped to match their wage.

steps.title: Why the workers' earlier discount does not count now
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא בריה דרב נתן spells out what we would have thought without רבי דוסא's line: the employer could pay a דינר less. רבי דוסא teaches that the workers can answer that they gave their discount only while it was not certain the employer would agree, so now they get a full סלע.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have thought the employer could say: 'You told me a דינר less, so I will give you a דינר less.' רבי דוסא teaches that the workers can answer: 'When we told you a דינר less, it was because things were not settled for you. Now they are settled.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing the answer from Step 17 by showing exactly what mistake רבי דוסא's line protects against.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The workers had agreed at the start to a דינר below the going rate. Without רבי דוסא's line, the employer could pay them a דינר less than the סלע they are owed. רבי דוסא teaches that the earlier discount belonged to the earlier situation, so the workers get the full סלע.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said (what we would have wrongly thought)
It is settled or certain for you

steps.whatToRemember: רבי דוסא's line "give them a סלע" is not obvious. It teaches that an early discount the workers agreed to cannot be used to cut their pay later.

phrases.english: You might have said:
"You told me a dinar less,
phrases.notes: This is the employer talking to the workers. A זוז is the same coin as a דינר.

phrases.english: so a dinar less is what I will give you,"
so it teaches us
that they can say to him:
"When we told you a dinar less,
that was when it was not certain for you;
phrases.notes: Back then it was not clear you would pay the higher wage. Now it is clear.

phrases.english: now it is certain for you."

steps.triggerLanguage: מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא: בְּצִיר זוּזָא אַמְרִיתוּ לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the answer from Step 17 by naming the wrong idea that רבי דוסא's line rules out.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the new teaching (חידוש) in a specific case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The employer could pay a דינר less for the remaining work, since the workers agreed to a discount.
steps.terutzMaskana: The workers can say the discount was given only while it was not certain the employer would agree, so he must give them a full סלע.

steps.title: רב rules like רבי דוסא
steps.stepSummary: רב rules that the הלכה follows רבי דוסא in the dispute about workers who back out.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: The הלכה follows רבי דוסא.
steps.whatsHappening: רב gives a practical ruling in the dispute from the ברייתא. This sets up the challenge that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי דוסא held that the worker who backs out takes the loss (Step 13). By ruling like him, רב seems to accept that the worker who quits loses out.

phrases.english: Rav said:
The halacha follows Rabbi Dosa.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After explaining רבי דוסא's opinion, the גמרא now brings a ruling that follows it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The הלכה follows רבי דוסא: the worker who backs out takes the loss.

steps.title: But רב says a worker can quit midday
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב's ruling with another statement of רב: a worker can back out even in the middle of the day.
steps.simpleTranslation: Did רב really say this? Didn't רב say: A worker can back out even in the middle of the day!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that רב seems to contradict himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי דוסא's opinion puts the loss on the worker who quits. But רב elsewhere protects the worker and lets him quit freely, even halfway through the day. These two positions seem to clash.

keyTerms.meaning: But did רב really say this?
To back out, to go back on his word

phrases.english: But did Rav really say this?
But didn't Rav say:
A worker can back out
even in the middle of the day!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי אָמַר רַב הָכִי? וְהָאָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב's ruling from Step 19 with another statement of רב.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling that the הלכה follows רבי דוסא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב's own statement lets a worker quit freely midday, which seems to clash with רבי דוסא's view that the worker who backs out takes the loss.

steps.title: Maybe רבי דוסא splits day-hire from contract work
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests an answer: רבי דוסא might treat a day-hire worker differently from a contract worker.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you will say that רבי דוסא makes a difference between day-hire work and contract work.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a possible way out of the contradiction. It does not accept it yet, and the next step will test it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case in the ברייתא was a job contract, a fixed price for the whole job. Maybe רבי דוסא only makes a contract worker lose when he quits. Then רב could still hold that a day-hire worker may quit freely, and there is no contradiction.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you will say (a suggested answer)
Contract work, paid for the whole job

steps.confusionAlert: The phrase וְכִי תֵימָא only offers an answer for discussion. It is not the גמרא's final word, and the very next line attacks it.

phrases.english: And if you will say
that Rabbi Dosa makes a difference
between day-hire work and contract work,

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא שָׁאנֵי לֵיהּ לְרַבִּי דּוֹסָא בֵּין שְׂכִירוּת לְקַבְּלָנוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Suggests an answer to the contradiction raised in Step 20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishes between two types of work
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב contradicts himself by ruling like רבי דוסא.
steps.terutzMaskana: Suggested: רבי דוסא makes only the contract worker lose, so רב's freedom to quit applies to the day-hire worker.

steps.title: Does רבי דוסא really split them? A ברייתא about a midday death or fever
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions whether רבי דוסא really makes this difference, and starts quoting a ברייתא about a worker who stops midday because of a death or a fever.
steps.simpleTranslation: But does he really make a difference? Wasn't it taught in a ברייתא: One who hires a worker, and in the middle of the day the worker heard that a relative of his died, or he was gripped with fever, if he is a day-hire worker...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the suggested answer by beginning to bring a ברייתא. This sets up a proof that is finished on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The suggested answer needs רבי דוסא to treat day-hire and contract work differently. The גמרא brings a ברייתא that discusses both kinds of worker who stop midday. The rest of it will show whether רבי דוסא really separates them.

phrases.english: But does he really make a difference?
But wasn't it taught in a baraita:
One who hires a worker,
and in the middle of the day
he heard that a relative of his died,
or he was gripped with fever,
if he is a day-hire worker —

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the suggested answer from Step 21 by beginning to quote a ברייתא.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The suggestion that רבי דוסא treats day-hire and contract work differently
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: A ברייתא about a worker who stops midday is brought to show that רבי דוסא may not separate the two kinds of work. The proof is finished in the continuation.
